mainTopic: Which measuring vessels a merchant may make so that people do not confuse close sizes, and שמואל's one-sixth limit on changing measures, coins and profit.
overview: This amud finishes a ברייתא that lists the measuring vessels a merchant may keep. It ends the dry measures with the tiny עוכלא, then lists the liquid measures from a הין down to a קורטוב. The גמרא asks why a two-קב vessel is left out and works out the rule that people confuse measures a quarter apart but not a third apart. It then explains two exceptions: people know small measures well, and the third-הין and quarter-הין were allowed because they were used in the מקדש, where the כהנים are careful. Next, שמואל teaches that measures, coin values and a seller's profit may not be raised by more than one-sixth. The גמרא tries three logical reasons for the limit on measures: rising prices, cancelled sales, and protecting the merchant. Each one is rejected. Finally, רב חסדא says שמואל learned the rule from a פסוק in יחזקאל, and the explanation of that פסוק continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The smallest dry measure: the עוכלא
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא ends its list of dry measures with the עוכלא and defines it as one-fifth of a quarter-קב.
steps.simpleTranslation: And an עוכלא. How much is an עוכלא? One-fifth of a quarter of a קב.
steps.whatsHappening: We are joining the ברייתא in the middle of its list of dry measuring vessels. It names the last and smallest one, the עוכלא, and tells us its size.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A quarter-קב divided into five gives one-twentieth of a קב. This tiny size will matter later, when the גמרא compares it to the half-תומן, which is one-sixteenth of a קב.

keyTerms.meaning: A small dry measure, one-twentieth of a קב
A quarter, here a quarter of a קב
A basic dry measure; larger and smaller measures are counted from it

phrases.english: And an ukla.
And how much is an ukla?
One-fifth of a quarter-kav.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא's list of dry measures from the previous section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An עוכלא equals one-fifth of a quarter-קב, which is 1/20 of a קב.

steps.title: The list of liquid measures
steps.stepSummary: For liquids, a merchant may make vessels of a הין, half-הין, third-הין, quarter-הין, לוג, half-לוג, quarter-לוג, eighth-לוג, and one-eighth of an eighth, called a קורטוב.
steps.simpleTranslation: For liquid measures, one may make a הין, a half-הין, a third of a הין, a quarter of a הין, a לוג, a half-לוג, a quarter, an eighth, and one-eighth of an eighth, which is a קורטוב.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא now switches from dry measures to liquid measures and lists every vessel size a merchant may make.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A הין is twelve לוג, so the third-הין is four לוג and the quarter-הין is three לוג. The list goes down to the קורטוב, which is 1/64 of a לוג. The גמרא will soon ask why the third-הין and quarter-הין may both be made, since they are so close in size.

keyTerms.meaning: A liquid measure equal to twelve לוג
The smallest liquid measure, 1/64 of a לוג

phrases.english: And in liquid measure, he makes a hin,
and a half-hin, and a third of a hin,
and a quarter of a hin, and a log, and a half-log,
and a quarter, and an eighth,
phrases.notes: These are a quarter and an eighth of a לוג, not of a הין.

phrases.english: and one-eighth of an eighth –
and this is a kortov.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the dry measures to the liquid measures in the same ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The permitted liquid vessels are the הין, half-הין, third-הין, quarter-הין, לוג, half-לוג, quarter-לוג, eighth-לוג, and קורטוב.
steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא gives a fixed list of permitted sizes. The rest of the section asks why certain sizes are missing from it, and why some close sizes are included.

steps.title: Why not make a two-קב measure?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the dry list leaves out a vessel of two קב.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him also make a two-קב measure!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא notices that a two-קב vessel is missing from the dry list and asks why it isn't allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The list includes a קב and a תרקב, which is three קב. Two קב seems like a natural size to include in between, so leaving it out needs an explanation.

phrases.english: And let him also make a two-kav measure!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about a size missing from the dry list.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's list of dry measures.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Two קב is an obvious, useful size, so why isn't it on the list?

steps.title: It could be confused with a תרקב
steps.stepSummary: A two-קב vessel might be mistaken for a תרקב, which is three קב.
steps.simpleTranslation: People would come to confuse it with a תרקב.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that a two-קב vessel was left out so that people would not mix it up with the three-קב תרקב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two קב and three קב differ by one-third of the larger vessel. The answer assumes that a gap that small could fool a buyer, who would end up getting less than he paid for.

keyTerms.meaning: Will come to be mixed up
A dry measure of three קב

phrases.english: It will come to be confused with a tarkav.
phrases.notes: A תרקב is three קב, so the worry is mixing up two with three.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the two-קב measure.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives a practical reason: the sizes could be confused.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Two קב seemed like a harmless size to add.
steps.terutzMaskana: It is left out because it could be confused with a three-קב תרקב.

steps.title: Then the קב itself should be banned too
steps.stepSummary: If people confuse sizes that differ by a third, a קב should also be banned, since it differs from a half-תרקב by a third.
steps.simpleTranslation: So it seems people make mistakes of a third. If so, he should not make a קב either, since it would be confused with a half-תרקב!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws a rule from the last answer and shows that the rule causes a problem: it would forbid the קב, which is on the list.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two versus three קב is a gap of one-third. A קב versus a half-תרקב, which is one and a half קב, is also a gap of one-third. So the reason given in step 4 would wrongly ban the קב as well.

keyTerms.meaning: Half a תרקב, one and a half קב

phrases.english: Apparently, people err by a third –

phrases.aramaic: אִי הָכִי, קַב נָמֵי לָא לֶיעְבֵּיד;
phrases.english: if so, he should not make a kav either;
since it will come to be confused with a half-tarkav!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a rule from the answer in step 4 and attacks it.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that two קב would be confused with a תרקב.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If a one-third gap causes confusion, the קב, which is listed, should be forbidden because of the half-תרקב.

steps.title: The real reason: confusion with a half-תרקב
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא changes its answer. A two-קב vessel is banned because it could be confused with a half-תרקב.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, this is the reason one does not make a two-קב measure: it would be confused with a half-תרקב.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops its first reason and gives a new one for why two קב is not allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two קב versus one and a half קב is a gap of one-quarter, which is smaller than a third. So the new rule is that people confuse sizes a quarter apart, but not a third apart. That rule bans two קב while still allowing the קב.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather; signals that the earlier answer is replaced

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the קב is banned now. The new rule is that only a quarter-sized gap causes confusion, and the קב is a third away from the half-תרקב, so it stays allowed.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא קַבַּיִים הַיְינוּ טַעְמָא דְּלָא עָבֵיד –
phrases.english: Rather, this is the reason he does not make a two-kav measure –
since it will come to be confused with a half-tarkav.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא קַבַּיִים הַיְינוּ טַעְמָא דְּלָא עָבֵיד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the answer of step 4 to avoid the problem raised in step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Replaces the earlier reason with a new comparison.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Two קב was banned because of the three-קב תרקב, a gap of one-third.
steps.terutzMaskana: Two קב is banned because of the half-תרקב, a gap of one-quarter. Only a quarter-sized gap causes confusion.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the working rule for the rest of the section: people can confuse measures a quarter apart.

steps.title: Then the half-תומן and עוכלא should be banned
steps.stepSummary: If people confuse a quarter-sized gap, then the half-תומן and the עוכלא, which are even closer, should not both be allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: So it seems a person errs by a quarter. If so, he should not make a half-תומן and an עוכלא!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא applies the new rule to the small dry measures and finds a problem with two sizes on the list.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A half-תומן is 1/16 of a קב and an עוכלא is 1/20 of a קב. The עוכלא is only a fifth smaller, which is closer than a quarter, yet the ברייתא allows both.

keyTerms.meaning: Half a תומן, 1/16 of a קב

phrases.english: Apparently, a person errs by a quarter –

phrases.aramaic: אִי הָכִי, חֲצִי תּוֹמֶן וְעוּכְלָא לָא לֶיעְבֵּיד!
phrases.english: if so, he should not make a half-tomen and an ukla!
phrases.notes: A half-תומן is 1/16 of a קב and an עוכלא is 1/20, so they are even closer than a quarter apart.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the quarter rule from step 6 against the small measures.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's permission to make both a half-תומן and an עוכלא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If a quarter-sized gap causes confusion, sizes that are only a fifth apart should certainly be confused.

steps.title: רב פפא: people know small measures well
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא answers that people are expert in small measures and do not confuse them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: people are experts in small measures.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא explains that the quarter rule does not apply to small vessels, because people can tell them apart.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry about confusion applies to large measures, where a difference is hard to see. With small vessels, people notice even a small difference in size, so the half-תומן and the עוכלא can both be allowed.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
People are expert in small measures.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא מִדּוֹת קְטַנּוֹת בְּקִיאִי בְּהוּ אִינָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the small measures.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the rule: it does not apply to small measures.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any two sizes a quarter apart or closer would be confused.
steps.terutzMaskana: Small measures are an exception, since people can tell them apart.

steps.title: Then the third-הין and quarter-הין should be banned
steps.stepSummary: The third-הין, which is four לוג, and the quarter-הין, which is three לוג, are a quarter apart, so one of them should be forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: A third of a הין and a quarter of a הין: he should not make them!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now applies the quarter rule to the liquid list and finds two sizes that should not both be allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Four לוג versus three לוג is a gap of one-quarter, exactly the gap that causes confusion. These are not small measures, so רב פפא's answer does not help here.

keyTerms.meaning: A third of a הין, four לוג
A quarter of a הין, three לוג

phrases.english: A third of a hin, a quarter of a hin –
let him not make them!

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁלִישִׁית הַהִין רְבִיעִית הַהִין לָא לֶיעְבֵּיד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the quarter rule against the liquid measures.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's permission to make both a third-הין and a quarter-הין.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Four and three לוג are a quarter apart and are not small measures, so they should be confused.

steps.title: Temple measures were not forbidden
steps.stepSummary: Since these measures were used in the מקדש, the רבנן did not make a גזירה against them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since they were used in the מקדש, the רבנן did not decree against them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the third-הין and quarter-הין are allowed because they were used in the מקדש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These sizes appear in the Temple service, for example for the wine and oil of the נסכים. Because they had that role, the רבנן did not ban them for ordinary use.

keyTerms.meaning: They decreed, made a rabbinic ban

phrases.english: Since they existed in the Temple,
the Sages did not decree against them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the third-הין and quarter-הין.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Exception: measures used in the Temple were not banned.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: These sizes should be banned like the two-קב vessel.
steps.terutzMaskana: Because they were Temple measures, the רבנן left them allowed.

steps.title: Why not ban them in the Temple too?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the רבנן did not make a גזירה against these measures even in the מקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let them decree in the מקדש too!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back: if the sizes can be confused, the same danger should exist in the מקדש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being used in the מקדש does not by itself stop people from mixing up sizes. So the רבנן should have banned them there too, and then they would not be an exception anywhere.

phrases.english: In the Temple too, let them decree!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that Temple use protects these measures from a ban.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The risk of confusion exists in the מקדש too, so the רבנן should have banned them there as well.

steps.title: Priests are careful
steps.stepSummary: There was no need for a ban in the מקדש, because כהנים are careful and would not confuse the measures.
steps.simpleTranslation: כהנים are vigilant.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ends the discussion: the כהנים who work in the מקדש are careful, so there was no fear of a mix-up there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The concern about confusion depends on who uses the vessels. Careful כהנים would not mix them up, so the רבנן made no ban in the מקדש. Since the sizes were in use there, they did not ban them elsewhere either.

keyTerms.meaning: Priests who serve in the Temple

steps.whatToRemember: The rule: people can confuse measures that are a quarter apart, so such sizes are not made. There are two exceptions: small measures, which people know well, and Temple measures, because כהנים are careful.

phrases.english: Priests are vigilant.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 11 and closes the discussion.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains that the people involved are careful, so the worry does not apply.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The mix-up concern should apply in the מקדש too.
steps.terutzMaskana: כהנים are careful, so no ban was needed there.

steps.title: שמואל's three one-sixth limits
steps.stepSummary: שמואל rules that measures, coins and a seller's profit may not be raised by more than one-sixth.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: You may not make the measures bigger by more than one-sixth. You may not raise the value of a coin by more than one-sixth. And a seller may not make a profit of more than one-sixth.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic with a teaching of שמואל that sets three limits, each of one-sixth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first limit is about a town changing its standard measures, so that the new measure holds more than the old one. The second is about raising the official value of a coin. The third limits how much profit a seller may take on what he sells.
steps.whyThisMatters: The rest of this section explores the reason for the first limit, the one on measures.

phrases.english: Shmuel said:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין מוֹסִיפִין עַל הַמִּדּוֹת יוֹתֵר מִשְּׁתוּת,
phrases.english: We may not add to the measures more than one-sixth,
phrases.notes: He means a town changing its standard measures so that they hold more than before.

phrases.english: and not to a coin more than one-sixth,
and one who profits should not profit more than one-sixth.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: אֵין מוֹסִיפִין עַל הַמִּדּוֹת יוֹתֵר מִשְּׁתוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new teaching, connected to the earlier discussion of measures.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Measures, coin values and a seller's profit may each be raised by up to one-sixth, but no more.

steps.title: Why the limit on measures?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא repeats the first rule and asks for its reason.
steps.simpleTranslation: We may not add to the measures more than one-sixth. What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the first part of שמואל's rule again and asks why it is so. This sets up a search for the reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is really two-sided. Why is adding one-sixth allowed at all, and why is adding more than one-sixth forbidden? Whatever reason is offered must explain both sides.

phrases.aramaic: אֵין מוֹסִיפִין עַל הַמִּדּוֹת יוֹתֵר מִשְּׁתוּת –
phrases.english: We may not add to the measures more than one-sixth —
what is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the first rule of step 13.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason that measures may be increased by up to one-sixth but not more.

steps.title: Rising prices cannot be the reason
steps.stepSummary: The suggestion that the rule prevents prices from rising is rejected, because then even one-sixth should be forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say the reason is that it makes market prices go up, then even one-sixth should not be allowed!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries a first reason, that changing measures pushes prices up, and right away knocks it down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Making the measures bigger by one-sixth would also push prices up. So if rising prices were the worry, any increase should be forbidden. This reason cannot explain why one-sixth is allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (a suggestion that is about to be rejected)

phrases.english: If you say it is because of raising market prices,
then one-sixth also should not be allowed!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִילֵּימָא מִשּׁוּם אַפְקוֹעֵי תַּרְעָא, שְׁתוּת נָמֵי לָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a first answer to step 14 and rejects it.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects rising prices as the reason for שמואל's rule.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: That reason would forbid even a one-sixth increase, but שמואל allows it.

steps.title: Second try: avoiding cancelled sales
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the limit exists so that sales are not cancelled because of אונאה, since only more than one-sixth cancels a sale.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the reason is because of אונאה, so that the sale will not be cancelled?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a second reason. The limit keeps the change small enough that a sale made by mistake with the old measure would not be cancelled.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under the laws of אונאה, a gap of less than one-sixth stands, a gap of exactly one-sixth must be paid back, and a gap of more than one-sixth cancels the sale. If measures grow by one-sixth at most, mix-ups between old and new measures will never cancel a sale. This would explain why one-sixth is the line.

keyTerms.meaning: Overcharging or underpaying compared to the fair price

phrases.english: Rather, it is because of overcharging —
so that there will not be a cancelling of the sale?
phrases.notes: Under the rules of overcharging, only a gap of more than one-sixth cancels a sale.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the reason rejected in step 15.
steps.terutzMaskana: The rule keeps changes within one-sixth so that mistaken sales are not cancelled.

steps.title: רבא: with measured goods, any mistake reverses the sale
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that for goods sold by measure, weight or count, even a gap smaller than one-sixth reverses the sale, so the one-sixth limit would not help.
steps.simpleTranslation: But רבא said: Anything sold by measure, by weight or by count is returned even if the gap is less than the amount of אונאה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the second reason by quoting רבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The one-sixth rule of אונאה only applies when the value is a matter of judgment. When goods are measured, weighed or counted, any shortfall is a clear mistake, and the sale is reversed. Since measures are exactly such a case, keeping the change under one-sixth would not save the sale.

keyTerms.meaning: But didn't he say? (introduces a challenge)
Goes back; the sale is reversed

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think רבא disagrees with the one-sixth rule of אונאה. He is saying that it only covers goods whose value must be estimated, not goods that are measured exactly.

phrases.english: But didn't Rava say:
anything that goes by measure, by weight, or by count —
even less than the amount of overcharging, it is reversed!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reason given in step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that the one-sixth limit prevents sales from being cancelled.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: With measured goods any error reverses the sale, so a one-sixth limit gives no protection.

steps.title: Third try: so the merchant suffers no loss
steps.stepSummary: The limit protects a merchant who keeps selling by the old measure, so that at worst he only loses his usual profit.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the reason is so that the merchant will not suffer a loss.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a third reason, that the limit protects the merchant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A merchant who has not heard about the new measure may keep selling by the old one. Since a merchant's normal profit is about one-sixth, a change of up to one-sixth only wipes out his profit and does not make him lose money.

phrases.english: Rather, so that there will not be a loss for the merchant.
phrases.notes: The worry is a merchant who doesn't know the measures changed and keeps selling by the old ones.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the reason rejected in step 17.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The limit was meant to prevent sales from being cancelled.
steps.terutzMaskana: The limit ensures a merchant using the old measure loses no more than his profit.

steps.title: A merchant needs a profit, not just no loss
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the third reason: protecting only against loss is not enough, since a merchant who earns nothing is not really a merchant.
steps.simpleTranslation: You made sure he suffers no loss, but doesn't he need a profit? Someone who buys and sells for nothing, is he called a merchant?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the third reason with a well-known saying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the חכמים wanted to protect merchants, saving them only from a loss is not enough. A one-sixth change would wipe out the merchant's whole profit. A merchant who buys and sells without earning anything is not doing business at all, so this reason looks weak.

phrases.english: Is it only a loss that he should not have —
doesn't he need a profit?!
Buy and sell — is that called a merchant?!
phrases.notes: This is a popular saying: buying and selling with no profit doesn't make you a merchant.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reason given in step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that the limit protects merchants from loss.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Real protection for merchants would also save their profit, which a one-sixth change completely wipes out.

steps.title: רב חסדא: שמואל's rule comes from a verse
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא drops the search for a logical reason. He says שמואל learned the one-sixth limit from a פסוק in יחזקאל that lists 20, 25 and 15 שקלים as making up one מנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב חסדא said: שמואל found a verse and expounded it: "And the שקל shall be twenty גרה; twenty שקלים, twenty-five שקלים, fifteen שקלים shall be your מנה."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives up on explaining שמואל's rule through logic and offers a פסוק as its source instead. This step quotes the פסוק, and the explanation of what it teaches continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 15 to 19 tried three logical reasons for the one-sixth limit, and each one was knocked down. The word אלא signals a fresh start: the rule is a דרשה from a פסוק, not a matter of reasoning. The פסוק lists 20, 25 and 15 שקלים, which add up to 60 שקלים for one מנה. The next amud shows how this number teaches the one-sixth limit.

keyTerms.meaning: He expounded, drew a lesson from the verse
A small coin or weight. Twenty make one shekel.
A larger unit of weight or money

steps.confusionAlert: Don't read the פסוק as three separate מנה amounts. The 20, 25 and 15 שקלים are added together to make one מנה of 60 שקלים.
steps.whyThisMatters: This changes the whole sugya. Once the rule rests on a פסוק, the earlier objections against the logical reasons no longer threaten it.

phrases.english: Rather, Rav Chisda said:
Shmuel found a verse and expounded it:
"And the shekel shall be twenty gera;
twenty shekels, twenty-five shekels,
fifteen shekels
shall be your maneh."
phrases.notes: Add them up: 20 + 25 + 15 = 60 שקלים in one מנה.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא: שְׁמוּאֵל קְרָא אַשְׁכַּח וּדְרַשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the failed logical reasons from steps 15 to 19 with a source in a פסוק.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shifts the basis of the rule from logic to a verse
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The one-sixth limit had to be explained by some practical reasoning about prices, cancelled sales or a merchant's profit.
steps.terutzMaskana: The limit is learned from the פסוק in יחזקאל that sets the מנה at 60 shekels.
